prior_narrative.tldr: This thread was regrouped from a broad 'large language models' reading list into reinforcement learning. Oct 15-23 papers centered on agentic RL environments, rollout budgets and credit assignment, with an AWS SageMaker guide for multi-turn RL.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 2-3: three more RL papers, including JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent framework for long-horizon web tasks, and EffComp, which trains prompt compression with RL.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Nearly all of this is research: the recurring cost levers are rollout budgets, scheduling and credit assignment, which decide what agent RL training costs and whether it is stable.
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you train agents with RL, try rollout-budget or scheduling ideas on your own cost curve and rerun your evals; treat these preprints as unreplicated until code and independent results appear.

beats.headline: Agentic RL gets benchmarks, rollout budgets and stateful environments
Credit assignment, rounding stability, user simulation and a SageMaker guide
beats.summary: Training-stability and credit-assignment papers, plus AWS's hands-on multi-turn RL guide.

beats.headline: Calibration, error-targeted fixes, co-evolving harnesses and rollout scheduling
Self-learning, sequence confidence, skill routing, flow policies and causal explanations
Prompt compression, open multi-agent theory and hierarchical web agents
beats.summary: Nov 2-3: three more RL papers, ending with a multi-agent framework for long-horizon web tasks.

open_questions: Do rollout-budget and scheduling gains hold on production-size agent workloads?
Does fine-grained credit assignment help beyond the video-editing setting where it also hurt?
Will any of these frameworks ship code that others can reproduce?
